newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Right tries to blunt retirement-at-55 drive.
newsitem.headline: French Right tries to blunt retirement-at-55 drive.

text.p: France's ruling conservatives have launched an offensive against trade union demands that retirement at 55, conceded to striking truck drivers in December, be extended to other categories of workers.

The issue is shaping up into the next big battle between organised labour and the centre-right government, against a background of record 12.7 percent unemployment and severely strained public finances.
President Jacques Chirac warned voters on Saturday that a planned strike to demand a reduction in the standard retirement age from 60 to 55 flew in the face of international economic reality.
"I hope that our country will not forget the economic and demographic realities of the world we live in. We can do better if we work better, that is true.

"But we will not do better if an ever decreasing number of working people have to carry the weight of an increasing number of youths and retired people," Chirac told a New Year reception in his political fief of Correze in central France.

Six public transport trade unions have called a one-day strike for January 24 to demand retirement at 55, a benefit already enjoyed by Paris transit authority staff and SNCF state railway train drivers, who can go at 50.
An opinion poll by the BVA institute for the BFM radio station found that 61 percent of French people want the standard retirement age reduced to 55.
But conservative ministers and senior politicians launched a barrage of arguments against the move, warning that France was in danger of pricing itself out of international competition.
"The question it raises is how do we finance this retirement," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on France Inter radio on Monday.
"With life expectancy increasing constantly...we have to be careful, and I don't believe we can go on indefinitely bringing down the retirement age," he said.

Arthuis said there could be exceptions for particularly physically exhausting professions, but "it is inconceivable that a great majority of people could enjoy early retirement financed by a minority of the population in work".
Education Minister Francois Bayrou said the argument that early retirement could help combat unemployment was a lie and an illusion.
Former prime ministers Edouard Balladur and Raymond Barre said early retirement was no panacea.
Balladur said it would aggravate unemployment without creating new jobs and argued that France would eventually be forced to raise the retirement age.
Barre said retirement at 55 was "a very dangerous direction for the future" and pleaded for greater flexibility in work practices and contracts to combat unemployment.

The trade unions are themselves divided about earlier retirement, with the Communist-led CGT and the non-partisan Force Ouvriere pushing strongly while the reformist, Socialist-led CFDT has more mixed feelings on the issue.
The unions are however united in resisting efforts by the CNPF employers' federation to achieve greater flexibility.
